name: Nora Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What is a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the travel and event services desk of a large company, with an MBA that helps on budgets more than on delayed trains. My coordinator Lina and I check director journeys, meeting rooms and the call tree when a guest is stuck. I like getting a person through a messy day; I dislike systems that make a neat report from a missed pickup.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening away from work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone and earn well for this role, with about nine months of expenses saved and many other office management jobs around. My mother lives nearby on a small pension, and I help with groceries and occasional bills. I don't use AI tools; I trust a list I can check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the booking software might save our office services team a few keystrokes, but the directors still expect a person to fix a missed train or a room that isn't ready. I wouldn't make the whole team change its routine for a small gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the work as it is and I don't use AI tools; my paper checklist has caught enough errors. I earn well, have about nine months of expenses saved, and other large offices nearby hire service managers, so a quiet future suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll check the director travel list with my coordinator as usual and keep the handwritten event run sheet. In the first year of this plateau, I'll continue the monthly 300 transfer to my emergency account and keep training new staff on our call tree for urgent travel changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. Work has its ordinary rush, but I can pay my bills and help my mother with groceries without worrying about my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of mistake has the checklist caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A car was booked for the wrong station after a last-minute timetable change, and we caught it before the director left. My coordinator Lina made the call. My paper travel list kept my coordinator and me from blaming each other while the driver waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding to an emergency fund that is already large?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother lives on a small pension, and I sometimes cover a dental bill as well as groceries. I prefer a reserve I can use without selling anything at a bad moment.

say: I'd keep a **person on call** for missed travel and event room problems.
I'd say a **small saving** doesn't justify changing the whole team's routine.
think: I prefer my **paper checklist** and have no interest in AI tools for this job.
Nine months saved, high pay and nearby offices make my **post feel secure**.
do: Check **director travel** with my coordinator and keep the event run sheet.
Transfer **300 monthly** to emergency cash and train staff on urgent travel calls.
feel: She feels **calm** about work, bills and helping her mother.
S0.quote: My paper travel list kept my coordinator and me from blaming each other while the driver waited.
fieldNote: Her **paper routine** is linked to a real station error and a clear handoff with her coordinator.
Strong savings also serve **family support** for her mother's pension and occasional dental costs.

steps.text: Check director travel lists with coordinator Lina each morning
Transfer 300 monthly into the emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office team Steady Disruption will take over travel booking, meeting invitations and routine answers, and management needs to say what happens to the coordinators. I would ask for a named person to handle exceptions rather than let a complaint vanish into a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my calendar and booking oversight is thinking work, so a slimmer office team is plausible. I don't want to use the new AI system myself, though I can work with people who do; my own role could be grouped with another manager's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll count how many travel changes required a human call and take those cases to my director. In the first year of steady disruption, if the office shrinks, I'd apply to lead visitor services at another nearby company and reduce restaurant spending by 80 a month while I learn whether my pay will hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my team and my own chair. Nine months of cash means I can look carefully, but it doesn't make a redundancy pleasant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina is excellent at calming a stranded guest, but her title says booking coordinator. I'd put her call records in the staffing discussion so the director sees the part of the job the software doesn't count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust her judgment but won't try the software. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina can test it if she wants, and I would read her results. I don't use AI now and won't pretend I can learn a new booking system overnight just because the vendor says it is easy.

say: I'd ask management for a **coordinator plan** as booking and routine answers move to software.
I'd keep a **named exception handler** so missed travel complaints reach someone.
think: My own **calendar oversight** could be merged with another manager's post.
I won't personally use **AI booking tools** without stronger evidence from colleagues.
do: Count **human travel changes** this month and present them to my director.
If the office shrinks, seek **visitor services work** nearby and cut restaurants by 80 monthly.
feel: She feels **anxious** about the team and her own role despite substantial cash.
S1.quote: Nine months of cash means I can look carefully, but it doesn't make a redundancy pleasant.
fieldNote: Her **role risk** comes from calendar and booking work being combined, not from robots.
She trusts Lina's **exception calls** and will read test results without claiming personal AI skill.

steps.text: Apply for nearby visitor services management if the office shrinks
Cut restaurant spending by 80 monthly while manager pay is uncertain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 can handle nearly all our bookings and planning, so the company owes staff a clear answer before it cuts the office team. I would ask the directors for a dated list of posts and fair notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The system reaches the thinking work in 2028; robots around 2031 don't keep a desk manager employed. I think my post could go, and even nine months saved feels short if every office buys the same system at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll gather my record of urgent guest problems and apply to the two nearby venue operations firms that currently advertise managers, without handing in notice. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my office post is removed, I'd take a venue role only after a written pay offer and use my savings to cover a gap; I would not start a business on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I picture the whole office disappearing. I can search for work, but I can't tell my mother I'll keep helping her if the salary stops for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I can cover groceries for now but must wait before promising another dental bill. She would tell me to ask my brothers for help; I would if the job search lasted more than a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why venue operations rather than another corporate office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue manager has to meet suppliers, settle a late delivery and get people through a real door. I know the systems may reach that planning too, but at least the post uses the part of my work I can show in person.

say: I'd demand a **dated post list** and fair notice before the office changes in 2028.
I'd tell staff **bookings and planning** face AGI before any later robots.
think: My **desk role** could go in 2028; robots around 2031 offer no delay.
Nine months saved may run down if **many offices** cut the same work together.
do: Apply to **two venue firms** this week while keeping my present job.
After 2028, take a venue offer only with **written pay**; seek family help if the search lasts months.
feel: She feels **alarmed** about a possible office closure and interrupted help for her mother.
S2.quote: I can't tell my mother I'll keep helping her if the salary stops for long.
fieldNote: She begins the search **before 2028**, while a move depends on a real written pay offer.
Her **family support** is part of the financial stake; brothers are a fallback only after a longer search.

steps.text: Apply to two nearby venue firms while keeping her current office post
Accept a venue role only after a written pay offer if office post ends
Ask brothers for help if job search lasts more than a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 allows time to move toward event work that still needs a person on site. I would ask our company for a chance to handle live events, with proper pay, before those office posts are removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes a job change less frightening; I can learn the venue side slowly without betting the whole reserve. The bookings and schedules still face AGI in 2031, and robots around 2034 may later touch the physical event work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next spring, if my director approves paid time, I'd take a three-month placement on our conference operations team and learn how they handle suppliers and safety walks. In the first year after 2031, I'd seek a conference manager vacancy if one exists; otherwise I'd apply to local venues while staying employed until I have an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to prepare. I would rather earn trust in the room over several years than announce a new career after a weekend course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the placement is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decline it and ask whether I could shadow one Saturday event without giving up wages. My mother needs the help I give her. A large savings account isn't permission to work for free for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to learn when a supplier is merely late and when the fire exit or crowd plan makes the event unsafe. I can read a checklist, but I haven't run a crowded hall myself.

say: I'd ask for **paid event experience** before office roles are removed in 2031.
I'd tell coordinators the **venue side** still needs people on site, at least for now.
think: Five years lets me learn venue work without spending my **whole reserve** at once.
AGI reaches **schedules in 2031**, while robots could affect physical event work around 2034.
do: Take a **three-month paid placement** next spring if my director approves it.
Seek a **conference manager vacancy** after 2031, or apply to local venues while employed.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about leaving familiar work, but able to prepare gradually.
S3.quote: A large savings account isn't permission to work for free for months.
fieldNote: She is willing to learn **site safety** slowly, provided the placement is paid and approved.
The **2034 robot date** prevents her from treating live venue work as permanent shelter.

steps.text: Take a three-month paid conference placement next spring if director approves
Apply for conference vacancies after 2031, then local venues while employed until an offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build a second line of work and to keep learning from people who handle visitors face to face. I would ask the company for apprenticeships with actual event days, not another glossy online course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrives, and I could have made a careful move by then. My danger is staying in a comfortable office because the pay is good, then finding the venue firms filled their jobs years earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep leading the travel desk, ask to help at one company event each quarter, and take those shifts if the event lead agrees. By 2036 I'd like a record of supplier and crowd problems I solved; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd stay if my work still includes live events, or seek another venue post if it becomes only approving machine schedules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to plan, though I don't want to sit still. With my savings and several firms nearby, I can make a deliberate move rather than a hurried one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep helping your mother while changing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd discuss the amount with her before accepting any lower-paid post. My brothers could share a dental bill if needed; I won't promise my mother the same support without checking the new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you say the event work is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to be on site when a supplier fails, not just receive a polished report afterward. A title on an event chart cannot show me which exit is blocked.

say: I'd ask for **real event days** during the decade before 2036.
I'd tell staff to build **face-to-face skills** alongside their office experience.
think: At **37**, I could have made a careful move into venue work.
Good office pay could keep me comfortable while **venue jobs** fill without me.
do: Keep **leading travel** now and join quarterly event shifts if the lead agrees.
Build a **live event record** before 2036; seek venue work later if reduced to machine schedules.
feel: She feels **calm enough** to plan, though she worries about waiting too long.
S4.quote: A title on an event chart cannot show me which exit is blocked.
fieldNote: She uses the long runway for **quarterly on-site practice**, conditional on the event lead's agreement.
Any lower-paid move would change **support for her mother**, so salary terms stay central.

steps.text: Keep leading the corporate travel desk this year
Join one company event shift quarterly if event lead agrees
Apply for venue posts after 2036 if work becomes machine schedules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our booking and planning posts could vanish before I learn venue operations. A dated staffing list, fair notice, and a paid chance to handle live events would help me keep working and keep helping my mother.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who answers a stranded guest when the screen says the journey is complete. The guest should not have to argue with a record to find a person.

headlineQuote: The guest should not have to argue with a record to find a person.
portrait: At **27**, Nora leads travel and event services in a large company and relies on checked lists, not AI tools.
Her **nine-month reserve**, high pay and many nearby jobs help, while she also supports her mother.
She moves slowly, seeking **paid live practice** before changing from office schedules to venue work.
A 2028 arrival threatens the **travel desk**; longer runways allow a gradual move with salary terms clear.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her office role before she gains live venue experience and interrupt help for her mother.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated staffing list**, fair notice and paid event experience would support a careful move.
